raw_case_text:
A 23-year-old woman presented to our hospital with a two-day history of fevers and vomiting, epigastric pain, malaise, and headache. Her past history included polycystic ovaries, gastritis with previous helicobacter eradication, and hypothyroidism. She had recently travelled to her country of birth, Pakistan, for eight weeks and had returned to Australia two days prior to admission. Two weeks after arriving in Pakistan, she developed nausea, vomiting, headache, anorexia, and myalgia. Abdominal ultrasound was normal and barium swallow demonstrated gastritis. She was managed with esomeprazole, zinc, and atorvastatin. On returning to Australia, in addition to ongoing nausea and headache, she developed fevers and epigastric pain. On presentation to our metropolitan hospital she was febrile with 39.9 C, pulse rate 96/min, blood pressure 108/72 mmHg, and respiratory rate 20/min. Physical exam revealed a soft abdomen with mild suprapubic tenderness. Rose spots were present on her anterior chest and no jaundice was noted. Her white cell count was normal, platelet count was mildly low, her C-reactive protein elevated, and she had mild transaminitis (see Table 1).
No abnormalities were detected on chest X-ray. The blood cultures grew Salmonella Typhi with resistance to ciprofloxacin and sensitivity to amoxicillin, ceftriaxone, and cotrimoxazole. Investigations for malaria, HIV, dengue, and viral hepatitis were all negative. Stool cultures were negative.
She was treated with intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g daily. On the third day of her admission she developed severe right upper quadrant pain with localised peritonism despite her fever settling. Her LFTs were further deranged and abdominal ultrasound showed thickening of the gallbladder with pericholecystic fluid and probe tenderness, consistent with acalculous cholecystitis (see Figure 1).
She underwent laparoscopic cholecystectomy on the dame day. During the operation, a swollen, oedematous, and nonperforated gall bladder without stones was noted. The liver was noted to be normal, and there was a small amount of free fluid in the pelvis. Culture of the bile was not performed.
The pathology of the resected gall bladder revealed chronic inflammatory cell infiltration and mild chronic cholecystitis (see Figures 2(a) and 2(b)).
She became febrile two days after the operation (temperature 38.8 C). Intravenous azithromycin was added to the antibiotic regime. A CT abdomen was unremarkable, and a chest X-ray revealed right lower lobe atelectasis. Intravenous meropenem was subsequently administered for the following two days. Her fever settled and she was discharged with oral azithromycin on day 10 of her admission.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 23-year-old woman presented with a 2-day history of fever, vomiting, epigastric pain, malaise, and headache following an 8-week trip to Pakistan.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Two weeks after arriving in Pakistan on an 8-week visit, the patient developed nausea, vomiting, headache, anorexia, and myalgia; an outpatient abdominal ultrasound was normal and a barium swallow showed gastritis, which was managed with esomeprazole, zinc, and atorvastatin. Two days after returning to Australia, her ongoing nausea and headache were complicated by new fevers, vomiting, malaise, and epigastric pain. On hospital day 3, despite defervescence on intravenous ceftriaxone, she developed severe right upper quadrant abdominal pain with localized peritonism.
subjective.past_medical_history: History of polycystic ovary syndrome, gastritis with prior Helicobacter pylori eradication, and hypothyroidism. Born in Pakistan; recently traveled to Pakistan for 8 weeks and returned to Australia 2 days before admission.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, nausea, vomiting, epigastric and subsequent severe right upper quadrant pain, anorexia, malaise, headache, and myalgia. Recent medications in Pakistan: esomeprazole, zinc, and atorvastatin.

objective.physical_examination: On presentation, temperature was 39.9 °C, pulse rate was 96/min, blood pressure was 108/72 mmHg, and respiratory rate was 20/min. She was anicteric with rose spots over her anterior chest and a soft abdomen with mild suprapubic tenderness. On hospital day 3, abdominal examination revealed severe right upper quadrant tenderness with localized peritonism.
objective.routine_investigations: Initial blood tests showed a normal white blood cell count, mild thrombocytopenia, elevated C-reactive protein, and mild transaminitis. Malaria, HIV, dengue, and viral hepatitis screens as well as stool cultures were negative. Admission chest X-ray was normal. On hospital day 3, liver function tests worsened, and abdominal ultrasound demonstrated gallbladder wall thickening, pericholecystic fluid, and sonographic Murphy's sign (probe tenderness) without gallstones, consistent with acute acalculous cholecystitis. Postoperative chest X-ray showed right lower lobe atelectasis.
objective.advanced_workup: Blood cultures grew Salmonella Typhi resistant to ciprofloxacin and susceptible to amoxicillin, ceftriaxone, and co-trimoxazole. Same-day laparoscopic cholecystectomy on day 3 revealed an edematous, swollen, non-perforated acalculous gallbladder, a normal liver, and minimal pelvic free fluid; histopathology of the resected gallbladder showed chronic inflammatory cell infiltration and mild chronic cholecystitis (bile culture was not performed). Postoperative abdominal CT was unremarkable.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Ciprofloxacin-resistant Salmonella Typhi typhoid fever complicated by acute acalculous cholecystitis, confirmed by blood culture with susceptibility testing, hepatobiliary ultrasonography, laparoscopic findings, and gallbladder histopathology. Malaria, dengue, HIV, and viral hepatitis were ruled out. She was initially treated with intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g daily and underwent emergency laparoscopic cholecystectomy on hospital day 3. When postoperative fever (38.8 °C) recurred 2 days after surgery, intravenous azithromycin was added followed by 2 days of intravenous meropenem. Her fever resolved, and she was discharged on hospital day 10 on oral azithromycin.
